body:
The maintainer asked for housekeeping that runs at startup and about weekly, over memberships, invites, lists, close_votes and the rest.

What an investigation of the current state found (2026-09-19), so this is not rebuilt on a wrong premise:

1. Dangling references are structurally impossible, and none exist. `db.connect()` has set `PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON` since the first server commit (cb16678), and every referencing column is declared REFERENCES. A probe that drove the real API (last member leaves a closed expenses list; sole member deletes their account) then queried every parent-missing case found 0 of each: memberships/close_votes/items/invites with no list, memberships/close_votes with no account.
2. There is no such thing as a deleted-but-present account. `accounts._delete_account_row` hard-deletes the account and everything hanging off it — memberships, close_votes, auth_tokens, account_settings, invites it created — inside one transaction the caller commits, so a partial deletion rolls back.
3. What does linger, and is almost certainly what was seen, is rows on a TOMBSTONED list: the departing member's membership row (kept deliberately by invites.leave so their other devices converge on the tombstone), their close_vote, and the list's invites. The same probe found 1 of each. They are cleared by the existing gc.run() once the 90-day tombstone retention passes: after gc.run(now+91d) every one of those tables was empty and every invariant clean.
4. The actual defect is WHEN the sweep runs. gc.maybe_run is called from exactly one place, routes/sync.py, at most once per 24h. A server whose clients are not syncing never sweeps at all, so expired sessions, dead invites and retention-expired tombstones accumulate indefinitely. server/README.md says "a cron job is optional", which only holds while clients sync.

So the work is a trigger fix plus a standing audit, not a new cascade for states that cannot occur:

- A housekeeping sweep that runs (a) on the first request of a server run, which is how a blueprint gets a startup hook — boot.py explains there is no real one, and server_settings.py already uses boot.current_boot_id() for exactly this; and (b) on an interval of about a week. The existing ~daily retention GC stays as it is.
- An integrity audit, read-only, reporting through the audit log (audit.record, ids only, never emails). Checks in the order the maintainer gave: rows referencing an account that is gone (invites.created_by, close_votes, account_settings, memberships, auth_tokens); invites past their life; lists with no participants; then the remaining tables — close_votes on a non-expenses list, close_votes by a non-member of a live list, live items on a tombstoned list, tombstones past retention that GC should already have taken.
- Repair policy: delete what is unambiguously dead and already GC's job (retention tombstones, dead invites, idle sessions). A live list with zero memberships is TOMBSTONED, not deleted, so devices converge the normal way and retention takes it later. Anything that violates an invariant which cannot currently be reached is REPORTED, not silently deleted: it would mean a bug elsewhere, and deleting the evidence is the wrong move. Say so in the docstring.
- Needs meta.last_audit_at (migration) and somewhere to record the boot id the sweep last ran for. server/README.md's GC section and the CLI get updated; a `shoppinglist audit` command to run the checks on demand is worth having next to `shoppinglist gc`.
title: Housekeeping: a sweep on the first request of a server run and about weekly, plus an integrity audit of every table
